title: Mineralocorticoids: Replace Aldosterone Without Overloading the Patient
bottomLine: Fludrocortisone replaces mineralocorticoid activity when primary adrenal insufficiency causes aldosterone deficiency. Dose adequacy is judged from volume status, postural symptoms, blood pressure and electrolytes; it does not replace the urgent glucocorticoid and fluid treatment required for adrenal crisis.
recognize: Mineralocorticoid deficiency can cause salt craving, volume depletion, postural hypotension, hyponatremia and hyperkalemia in primary adrenal insufficiency.
Over-replacement can present with hypertension, edema or hypokalemia rather than improved adrenal symptoms.
differentiate: Primary adrenal insufficiency can impair both cortisol and aldosterone production; central or secondary adrenal insufficiency usually preserves the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and therefore does not routinely require mineralocorticoid replacement.
Fludrocortisone is chronic replacement therapy for mineralocorticoid deficiency, not the primary rescue drug for acute adrenal crisis.
assessment: Assess supine and standing blood pressure, dizziness, salt craving, hydration, edema, weight trend, current glucocorticoid regimen, adherence and medications that alter potassium or volume status.
Look for clinical evidence of under-replacement and over-replacement rather than titrating from one laboratory value in isolation.
workup: When the patient is stable, use the adrenal-insufficiency diagnostic pathway to establish primary disease and assess mineralocorticoid deficiency; renin, aldosterone and electrolytes can support the replacement plan.

During suspected adrenal crisis, obtain urgent electrolytes, glucose and cause-directed testing when feasible but do not delay immediate glucocorticoid treatment and fluid resuscitation for confirmatory testing.
management: Use oral fludrocortisone for confirmed mineralocorticoid deficiency and individualize replacement to symptoms, postural blood pressure, volume status and biochemical response.

If hypertension develops on replacement, reassess mineralocorticoid excess and other causes; dose reduction may be appropriate, while persistent hypertension can still require antihypertensive treatment without automatically abandoning necessary replacement.
Adrenal crisis requires emergency parenteral glucocorticoid therapy, isotonic fluid resuscitation and treatment of the precipitating cause according to acute-care guidance.
medicationSafety: Fludrocortisone can contribute to sodium and fluid retention, hypertension and hypokalemia; excessive dose escalation can therefore worsen cardiovascular risk.

Diuretics, mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonists and other drugs that alter potassium or volume status can complicate assessment of replacement adequacy; hypokalemia also increases the clinical hazard of drugs such as digoxin.
Do not confuse fludrocortisone with mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonists such as spironolactone or eplerenone, which block rather than replace mineralocorticoid activity.
redFlags: Hypotension or shock with suspected adrenal crisis
Persistent vomiting or inability to retain oral steroid therapy
Altered mental status or severe weakness with electrolyte disturbance
Severe hypertension, pulmonary edema or clinically important hypokalemia during replacement
counselling: Teach that mineralocorticoid replacement and glucocorticoid replacement have different jobs: fludrocortisone supports salt and volume balance, while the glucocorticoid plan must still be adjusted during physiologic stress.

Ensure the patient has a written sick-day plan, knows when urgent parenteral glucocorticoid treatment is needed, and does not simply increase fludrocortisone to manage fever, vomiting or severe illness.
followUp: Reassess postural symptoms, blood pressure, edema, weight and electrolytes after clinically meaningful dose or health-status changes, and use renin when appropriate to support longitudinal titration.
Coordinate endocrinology follow-up when replacement remains difficult to balance, pregnancy changes physiology, recurrent crises occur or the diagnosis is uncertain.
examTrap: Treating hypotension and vomiting in a patient with known primary adrenal insufficiency by increasing oral fludrocortisone and waiting for laboratory confirmation instead of recognizing adrenal crisis and giving immediate stress-dose glucocorticoid therapy with fluids.
oneLinePearl: Fludrocortisone manages aldosterone deficiency; adrenal crisis is a glucocorticoid-and-resuscitation emergency.
